subtopics.title: Index Overview and Methodology
subtopics.summary: The World Press Freedom Index is an annual report published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a non-profit organisation with headquarters in Paris. It has been published annually since 2002, and the 2026 edition is the 24th. The Index ranks 180 countries and regions on the level of freedom available to journalists, using a Press Freedom Questionnaire with five categories. Each country receives a score from 0 (worst) to 100 (best).
facts: Published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), a non-profit organisation
RSF was founded in 1985 and has its headquarters in Paris, France
Annual report since 2002; the 2026 edition is the 24th
Ranks 180 countries and regions by freedom available to journalists
Evaluates pluralism, media independence, legal framework and journalist safety
Press Freedom Questionnaire covers 5 categories
Each country gets a score from 0 (worst) to 100 (best)
Aim: safeguarding the right to freedom of information

subtopics.title: Key Findings and Country Rankings 2026
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Index finds that global press freedom has declined, with 52.2 per cent of countries rated 'Difficult' or 'Very Serious' for journalism. Only 1 per cent of the world's population lives in countries rated 'Good'. Norway remains top-ranked, while Syria recorded the sharpest rise after its political transition and Niger the steepest fall. The Middle East and North Africa remained the most dangerous region for journalists.

subtopics.title: Challenges and Significance of a Free Press
subtopics.summary: Media in 160 of the 180 countries face financial instability, which threatens independent and unbiased reporting, and political instability is linked to declining media freedom. A free press is often described as the fourth pillar of democracy, giving voice to marginalised communities and sparking debate that can lead to reform. During the pandemic, media acted as a critical communication tool between governments and citizens. Under the Indian Constitution, press freedom flows from Article 19(1)(a) but remains subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
facts: Media in 160 of 180 countries face financial instability
Political instability is linked to decline in media freedom
Press is often called the 4th pillar of democracy, alongside legislature, judiciary and executive
Press acts as a bridge between the governed and the governing, especially for marginalised communities

During the pandemic, media was a critical communication tool between government and citizens
Freedom of press is treated as part of freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a)
Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions, including on defamation, contempt of court and public order
Freedom of media is not an absolute freedom
In Romesh Thappar vs State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court said freedom of press lies at the foundation of all democratic organisations

subtopics.title: History and Institutions of Press Freedom in India
subtopics.summary: Printing in India expanded under European trading companies, and India's first newspaper, the Bengal Gazette, appeared in 1780. Colonial measures such as the Censorship of Press Act 1799 and the Vernacular Press Act 1878 restricted the press, while Metcalfe's Press Act 1835 is remembered as the liberator of the Indian press. Today, the Press Council of India, set up under the Press Council Act 1978, and the Editors Guild of India work to uphold press freedom and journalistic standards.

James Augustus Hickey's Bengal Gazette, India's first newspaper, was published in 1780

Bombay Samachar (1822), India's oldest running vernacular newspaper, was founded by Fardoonji Murazban
Metcalfe's Press Act 1835 is known as the liberator of the Indian press
Vernacular Press Act 1878, proposed by Lord Lytton, was enacted to suppress press freedom and criticism of British rule
Press Council of India was initially established in 1966 under the Indian Press Council Act 1965
Press Council of India was abolished in 1975 during the Emergency, after repeal of the 1965 Act
Press Council of India was established in 1978 as a statutory quasi-judicial body under the Press Council Act 1978

quizzes.title: Rankings and Key Findings 2026
quizzes.passage: Reporters Without Borders (RSF) has released the World Press Freedom Index 2026, the 24th edition of its annual report. The Index measures the level of freedom available to journalists in each country and region, and this year it covers 180 countries. Rankings are shaped by legal protections, the diversity of media outlets and the extent of political interference. Each country receives a score on a fixed scale, and the results show sharp contrasts. Some states remain at the top of the table, while others sit at the bottom with severe restrictions on reporters. Between these extremes, many countries have moved up or down because of changes in government or pressure on news organisations. Regions also differ greatly, and journalists in some parts of the world face far greater danger than others. Analysts often look first at the countries near the top and bottom, but the middle of the table also shows how legal and economic conditions change over time. The national questionnaire behind the Index asks experts about the political, legal, economic, social and security environment in each country. The report is widely read because it allows citizens to compare their own country with others. Its findings suggest that a free press is closely linked to informed public debate in any society.

quizzes.title: History of the Indian Press
quizzes.passage: Printing reached India through European trading companies, and for a long time newspapers were produced by colonial interests and Indian reformers alike. Colonial governments were uneasy about printed criticism. At different times they introduced rules to control what could be published, and some of these rules fell hardest on publications written in Indian languages. Even so, Indian editors kept bringing out weeklies that promoted social reform and nationalist ideas. Reformers used the press to challenge customs and argue for change in society. Over time, the limits on the press became a question for the courts and the constitution. Debates about press freedom focused on how expression could be balanced with public order and the rights of others. Later, statutory and non-statutory bodies were set up to watch over journalism and protect editorial standards, while professional associations of editors took up the defence of journalists' rights. Studying this history explains why modern India treats press freedom as important yet not absolute, and why the state and the press continue to debate where the limits should lie. The sequence of laws and institutions shows a long pattern in which governments tried to restrict the press while journalists sought wider freedom.
